title: Firefox
wiki_lead:
Mozilla Firefox, or simply Firefox, is a free and open-source web browser developed by the Mozilla Foundation and its subsidiary, the Mozilla Corporation. It uses the Gecko rendering engine to display web pages, which implements current and anticipated web standards. The software is available for Windows, macOS, and Linux systems, as well as a mobile version for Android (see Firefox for Android) and iOS, with unofficial ports for other platforms such as Oracle Solaris and OpenIndiana.
Firefox is the spiritual successor of Netscape Navigator, as the Mozilla community was created by Netscape in 1998, before Netscape's acquisition by AOL. Firefox was created in 2002 under the codename "Phoenix" by members of the Mozilla community who desired a standalone browser rather than the Mozilla Application Suite bundle. During its beta phase, it proved to be popular with its testers and was praised for its speed, security, and add-ons compared to Microsoft's then-dominant Internet Explorer 6. It was released on November 9, 2004, and challenged Internet Explorer's dominance with 60 million downloads within nine months. In November 2017, Firefox began incorporating new technology under the codename "Quantum" to promote parallelism and a more intuitive user interface.
The current version of Firefox is available for Windows 10 or later versions of Windows, as well as macOS and Linux. Its unofficial ports are available for various Unix systems such as Oracle Solaris and OpenIndiana, as well as for Unix-like operating systems, including FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, and other operating systems, such as ReactOS. It is the default, pre-installed browser on Debian, Ubuntu, and some other Linux distributions. Firefox is also available for Android and iOS. However, as with all other iOS web browsers, the iOS version uses the WebKit layout engine instead of Gecko due to platform requirements. An optimized version was also available on the Amazon Fire TV as one of the two main browsers available with Amazon's Silk Browser until April 30, 2021, when Firefox was discontinued on that platform.
Firefox usage share grew to a peak of 32.21% in November 2009, with Firefox 3.5 overtaking Internet Explorer 7, although not Internet Explorer as a whole; its usage then declined in competition with Google Chrome. As of July 2026, according to StatCounter, it has a 6.3% usage share on traditional PCs (i.e. as a desktop browser), making it the third-most popular PC web browser after Google Chrome (72%) and Microsoft Edge (10%), and ahead of Safari (5.2%).

grok_lead: Firefox is a free and open-source web browser developed by the Mozilla Foundation and its subsidiary, the Mozilla Corporation, emphasizing user privacy, security, and an open internet. Launched on November 9, 2004, with version 1.0, Firefox introduced innovative features like tabbed browsing, pop-up blocking, and integrated search, quickly gaining popularity as an alternative to dominant browsers like Internet Explorer. Backed by the non-profit Mozilla, it prioritizes internet health by avoiding the sale of user data to advertisers and promoting web standards. Firefox can be downloaded from the official Mozilla download page at https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/new/, which uses secure HTTPS and is provided directly by Mozilla. The browser's origins trace back to the late 1990s, when Netscape Communications open-sourced its browser codebase in 1998, leading to the formation of the Mozilla project in 1999. Early versions, such as Phoenix (2002) and Firebird (2003), evolved into Firefox, which by 2008's version 3.0 achieved a Guinness World Record for the most downloads in a single day at over 8 million. Major milestones include its mobile debut in 2010 on the Nokia N900, the 2017 release of Firefox Quantum that doubled performance and reduced memory usage by 30%, and ongoing privacy enhancements like Enhanced Tracking Protection in 2018 and Total Cookie Protection in 2022. These developments helped Firefox challenge browser monopolies, reducing Internet Explorer's market share from over 90% in the early 2000s to about 50% by 2010. Key features define Firefox's appeal, including a built-in password manager for secure storage and cross-device syncing, with official support for exporting saved logins to a CSV file via the logins manager (accessed through about:logins or Firefox menu > Passwords). To export, users open the Passwords page, click the three-dot menu, select Export Passwordsâ¦, confirm the warning that passwords will be unencrypted in the file, authenticate if required (via Primary Password or OS login), and save the.csv file. The exported CSV contains readable (unencrypted) passwords, so it must be handled securely, not shared, and deleted after use. A bookmark manager for organizing sites, and Private Browsing mode that blocks trackers and avoids saving history. Users can extensively customize the interface with themes and layouts, while the ecosystem supports thousands of extensions via the official add-ons store to add functionality like ad-blocking or productivity tools. Firefox Sync ensures seamless access to bookmarks, passwords, and tabs across desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux) and mobile (Android, iOS) platforms. As of 2026, Firefox continues to evolve with regular updates. Version 148, released on February 24, 2026, introduced an AI controls section in desktop settings. This feature provides users with a "Block AI enhancements" toggle to disable all generative AI features system-wide, as well as individual toggles for features such as AI-powered translations, alt text generation in PDFs, AI-enhanced tab grouping, link previews, and sidebar AI chatbots. In May 2026, version 151 introduced a major overhaul with a redesigned start page featuring customizable background images, enhanced tracking protection against fingerprinting, an updated PDF viewer capable of merging multiple documents, and a built-in VPN with location selection. Private browsing now includes a flame icon to instantly end a session without closing the window. In September 2026, Firefox 157 was rolled out with a redesigned interface across desktop and mobile, adding a more modern visual design, compact mode and greater customisation, as Mozilla sought to attract a wider audience beyond its traditional base of privacy and open-web advocates and position the browser as a stronger alternative to Chrome, Edge and Safari. The browser focuses on speed, security, and support for modern web technologies like WebXR, maintaining its role as a privacy-focused competitor in a market dominated by Google Chrome. Its commitment to open-source principles has influenced web standards, including contributions to codecs like AV1 and HTML5 advancements.
